ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Methods: Adults undergoing cardiac surgery were randomised 1:1:1:1 with concealed allocation to no treatment (Controls), sodium valproate 15mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks, 15mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks, or 25mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks pre-surgery.

> Results: The analysis cohort included 42 participants enrolled between January 2020 and August 2024.

> Participants were randomised with concealed allocation using Sealed Envelope in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to: 1.

> The protocol was registered prospectively (NCT03825250). (11) All participants had provided informed consent, and ethical approval was obtained prospectively from the East Midlands Research Ethics Committee (18/EM/0188).

> Adult cardiac surgery patients (≥18 years) undergoing cardiac surgery (CABG, Valve, or CABG and Valve) able in the opinion of the investigator, and willing to give informed consent were eligible.

> However, in our experience, the routine collection of adequate quantities of atrial myocardium is more consistent and reproducible than for ventricular tissue which is a key consideration in experimental RCTs where the numbers of participants are limited.

> All 10 control participants had concentrations at the limit of detection, confirming no off-protocol exposure.

Ethics approval statement:

> The protocol was registered prospectively (NCT03825250). (11) All participants had provided informed consent, and ethical approval was obtained prospectively from the East Midlands Research Ethics Committee (18/EM/0188).

> Anonymised clinical and biomarker data from the VALCARD study will be made available for ethically approved research with agreement from the study sponsor.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: A dose-finding trial evaluated safety and adherence for pre-cardiac surgery administration of sodium valproate.
Analyses of myocardium obtained from participants at surgery investigated mechanisms underlying treatment effects.

Methods: Adults undergoing cardiac surgery were randomised 1:1:1:1 with concealed allocation to no treatment (Controls), sodium valproate 15mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks, 15mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks, or 25mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks pre-surgery.
The primary analysis evaluated adherence and toxicity.
Myocardial injury was defined by high sensitivity serum troponin post-surgery.
Myocardial biopsies were analysed with single-nucleus Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin with sequencing (snATACseq), single nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNAseq), and immunofluorescence staining.
Candidate mechanisms were validated in vitro.
Results: The analysis cohort included 42 participants enrolled between January 2020 and August 2024.
Sodium valproate 15mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks had the highest levels of complete treatment adherence (70%), without severe drug related adverse effects.
Noncompliance (12/32, 38%) was increased with longer and higher dosing.

An as-treated analyses demonstrated a trend towards lower troponin release in participants receiving Valproate≤14 days (n=11) where myocardial biopsies demonstrated activation of pAKT-GSK3β, acetylation of p53 (K382) and GPX4 ferroptosis protection pathways versus controls (n=12).
Silencing of p53 attenuated the ferroptosis protective effect of valproate in vitro.
Treatment effects were not explained by changes in chromatin accessibility.
Treatment >14 days (n=19) was associated with cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, suppression of ferroptosis protection pathways, and increased myocardial injury.

text.text: Conclusions: Valproate 15mg/kg/day for ≤14 days pre-surgery is well tolerated in adults awaiting cardiac surgery and is associated with ferroptosis protection and lower troponin release.
Stage 4 CKD, chronic atrial fibrillation, a platelet count ≤150x10 9 .ml -1 , liver disease, or a recognised contra-indication to sodium valproate were ineligible.
Participants were randomised with concealed allocation using Sealed Envelope in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to: 1.
Standard care (no treatment) 2.

Sodium valproate at a target dose of 25 mg/kg per day for 4-6 weeks pre-surgery.
Sodium Valproate was administered as a twice daily oral dose for 1-6 weeks pre-surgery.
To minimise toxicity all participants commenced at 10mg/kg/day with dose escalation by 2.5mg/kg/day (max 200mg) every three days to achieve the target dose as specified in the treatment allocations.
Flexibility in target treatment duration anticipated up to 30% of elective cardiac surgery procedures being rescheduled at short notice to reduce protocol non-compliance.
Participants in the control arm received standard care; no treatment.

Safety and toxicity evaluations included baseline measurement of blood counts with assessment of hepatic and renal function, plasma valproate levels and full blood counts at baseline and after every two weeks of treatment.
Participants underwent twice weekly telephone call-based monitoring during the intervention period to assess compliance and adverse effects, and to advise on dose escalation.
Dose escalation was based on assessments of tolerance and likely adverse effect as follows: 1.
Patients experiencing no adverse effects were advised to continue dose escalation.

Patients with Class I Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE, https://evs.nci.nih.gov/ftp1/CTCAE/About.html) adverse events were advised to continue at the current dose if tolerated or to reduce the dose if not.

Perioperative myocardial injury affects >25% of cardiac surgery procedures where it is the primary cause of early death, or results in delayed recovery, lower quality of life, and increased healthcare resource use.( 1) Decades of research have not delivered effective myocardial protection interventions. (2) (3) (4) (5) (6) Sodium valproate is a class I/IIa Histone Deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi) in widespread use for the treatment of neurological diseases that protects myocardium from acute metabolic stress in a wide range of pre-clinical models. (7) We hypothesised that pre-surgery administration of sodium valproate would have myocardial protection effects in people exposed to the severe metabolic stress of cardiac surgery.

text.text: Valproate has unpredictable pharmacodynamics where in vivo effectiveness is not directly attributable to plasma concentrations.
Valproate also has both predictable (GI symptoms, reduction in platelet counts) and unpredictable (hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis) toxicity that affect adherence and safety.
The trial was designed as a dose finding study with pre-specified adherence, safety, and pharmacodynamic outcomes.

Based on the known biological effects of valproate, experimental analysis investigated whether treatment effects were attributable to changes in chromatin accessibility, (8) pro-survival gene expression, (7) (8) (9) or posttranscriptional modification of cellular injury responses (10) in myocardial biopsies from trial participants.

The protocol was registered prospectively (NCT03825250). (11) All participants had provided informed consent, and ethical approval was obtained prospectively from the East Midlands Research Ethics Committee (18/EM/0188).

Trial recruitment was terminated after the completion of the dose finding phase in September 2024 due to exhaustion of funds.
Adult cardiac surgery patients (≥18 years) undergoing cardiac surgery (CABG, Valve, or CABG and Valve) able in the opinion of the investigator, and willing to give informed consent were eligible.

A pre-specified secondary analysis explored pharmacodynamics, specifically doseresponses versus biomarkers of myocardial and kidney injury estimated from Area Under the Curve from baseline to 96 hours postoperatively for high sensitivity serum Troponin I (hsTroponin I) concentrations Human Cardiac Troponin I ELISA Kit (ab200016, Abcam, Cambridge, UK) and serum creatinine.
Adverse events were as defined by CTCAE, other than those included in the primary and secondary endpoints.

text.text: Baseline characteristics were presented by descriptive statistics, using mean and standard deviation (SD) for continuous data, and frequency (N) and percentage (%) for binary and categorical data in the full analysis set (FAS).

One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Pearson's chi-square χ2 test were used to investigate the differences in baseline characteristics among the four groups for continuous and binary/categorical variables, respectively.

Safety and toxicity endpoints (thrombocytopenia and hepatotoxicity) were analysed in all participants who at least took one dose of the randomised treatment (safety population set, SAF) and summarised by descriptive statistics.

Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) were used to explore the population average of the treatment effect (group effect), time effect, and the interaction between treatment and time effects on serum high-sensitivity troponin and serum creatinine measured across several time points from baseline to 6 weeks after cardiac surgery.
All statistical analyses were performed in Stata 18.

The study was reported as per the CONSORT Dose-finding Extension. (14) Due to high levels of non-adherence to valproate treatment the mechanism sub study used an as-treated approach that was not pre-specified in the trial protocol.

text.text: The as-treated grouping was defined before examining any outcome data.

As non-adherence with higher doses and longer treatment resulted in comparable drug exposure in the valproate 15mg/day for 4-6 weeks and the 25mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks groups, these were considered as a single group in the as-treated analyses, leaving three Groups for the as-treated comparison; Controls receiving no valproate, valproate ≤14 days, and valproate>14 days.

Continuous variables were analysed using one way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc group comparisons versus controls and Holm adjustment for multiple comparisons.
For single-nuclei ATAC sequencing, nuclei isolation and library construction used the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell ATAC Library kit v1.1. (10x Genomics).
Briefly, nuclei were re-suspended at the required concentration for the desired targeted nuclei recovery and transposed using a transposition mix.
Transposed nuclei were loaded on Chromium H Chip and the instrument run.
After library construction, a unique sample index was added to each sample.
Following quality control, libraries were purified and eluted using Buffer EB and SPRI select beads, with sequencing as described above, and bioinformatic analyses as described below.

Raw multiome sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger ARC v2.1.0 (10x Genomics) and aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38-2024-A) using default parameters, generating fragment files, peak accessibility matrices and quality metrics were generated for each sample.
Chromatin accessibility data was analysed in R (v4.4.2) using the Signac (15) and Seurat (16) packages.

Cell type annotation was performed using a reference-based approach, using a human cardiac reference atlas (SCP1849; ICM_scportal_05.24.2022.h5ad), with transfer anchors identified and cell identities predicted using Seurats FindTransferAnchors function and MapQuery functions.

text.text: To avoid pseudoreplication from treating nuclei as independent observations, all differential analyses were done at the donor level.
Cardiomyocyte (CM) and endothelial cells (ECs) were analysed separately.
For each cell type and modality, the raw count matrix was summed across nuclei within each donor by sparse matrix multiplication.
This gave one pseudobulk profile per donor: DecontX-corrected UMI counts per gene for snRNA-seq, and fragment counts per peak for snATAC-seq.
Donors contributing fewer than 10 nuclei, or with a pseudobulk library below 5,000 counts, were excluded.
Sex was included as a covariate when both sexes were represented among the retained donors and the resulting design matrix (~ sex and group) was of full rank, otherwise the model was ~ group.
RNA and ATAC libraries were prepared from separate aliquots of the same nuclei suspension from each donor.
Peaks were annotated using ChIPseeker (v1.38.0) with the TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene annotation database (19), with promoters defined as ±2kbp around an annotated TSS.

For each nucleus, the number of accessible peaks was counted in each class with a peak counted as accessible if it had at least one fragment.
These counts were then averaged per donor.
Donor means were compared across the three groups with the Kruskal-Wallis test and summarised as the median across donors.

text.text: A first-in-man evaluation of the HDACi sodium valproate in cardiac surgery, combined with multilevel characterisation of myocardial biopsies from trial participants and complementary in vitro experiments, suggests a myocardial protection effect of ≤14 days valproate treatment pre-surgery that is associated with activation of pAKT-pGSK3β (Ser9), acetylation of nuclear p53 (K382), and anti-ferroptosis GPX4 signalling in myocardium.
In vitro, valproate prevented ferroptosis in AC16 cardiomyocytes in response to IRI by activation of the p53/ TIGAR/ GPX4 pathway.

In contrast, valproate treatment >14 days was associated with cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, suppression of ferroptosis protection signaling, increased expression of necroptosis, apoptosis and ferroptosis susceptible networks, and increased myocardial injury post-surgery.

text.text: The effects of valproate ≤14 days were not explained by changes in chromatin accessibility, which likely reflect the short drug exposure in the trial.
This is also consistent with our results showing the main effectors as post-transcriptional.

text.text: Both are targets of the PPARα/PGC-1α axis that governs mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation.

One of the principal non-epigenetic actions of valproate is inhibition of β- oxidation through sequestration of free coenzyme A and carnitine.( 33) Inhibition of fatty acid oxidation in the adult heart promotes a less differentiated, more regeneration-competent cardiomyocyte state. (34) The accompanying reduction in myofilament accessory and M-band transcripts, without change in the core contractile genes, is consistent with this partial, reversible shift in cardiomyocyte phenotype rather than with loss of contractile apparatus.

text.text: We observed this combined signature only with ≤14 days of treatment, alongside the cytoprotective signals described above, and it was absent after longer exposure.
Third, participants treated >14 days showed loss of SYNE1, a critical regulator of nuclear cytoskeletal mechanotransduction.

text.text: Loss of SYNE1 is associated with a cardiomyopathy phenotype and increased susceptibility to injury through pro-apoptotic p53 target genes, consistent with our results.( 35) Together, these observations suggest that the early metabolic and cytoprotective adaptations to valproate are not sustained, and that prolonged exposure is accompanied by a distinct changes that increase myocardial injury susceptibility.

Ferroptosis is increasingly recognised as an important therapeutic target for the prevention of IRI in humans.( 36) However, there are currently no licensed clinical therapeutics for ferroptosis in humans. (37) Our results provide new evidence that ferroptosis is an important contributor of myocardial cell death following cardiac surgery.

text.text: In addition, we show that valproate, a widely available, inexpensive, generic medication that is well tolerated by people waiting for surgery, is associated with increases in ferroptosis protection pathways and likely reduced troponin release in vivo.
Future research will evaluate whether valproate pretreatment results in clinically significant reductions in myocardial injury via attenuation of ferroptosis.
First, the ITT analysis did not demonstrate a treatment effect, and the as-treated analysis will have introduced significant bias, given our knowledge of the ITT results.
In mitigation, using an ITT approach, when 38% of participants did not receive their minimum required treatment for the mechanistic analysis, would have introduced greater bias.

The value of this approach was demonstrated by consistent findings across the as-treated analysis of troponin release and myocardial injury, multilevel characterisation of myocardial biopsies, and in vitro experiments.
However, our findings cannot be considered causal as a result.
Second, the trial was terminated after completion of the experimental medicine and dose finding phase due to the exhaustion of available funds caused by the COVID19 pandemic.
Progression to a proof-of-concept efficacy trial is warranted based on these results.
Third, our pseudobulk analyses of snRNAseq and snATACseq were underpowered to determine treatment effects on chromatin accessibility and gene expression.

We adopted rigorous quality control to mitigate the risk of ambient RNA contamination arising from fracturing of cardiomyocyte nuclei during freeze-thawing, but after quality control only 3 to 9 donors per group contributed to each pseudobulk analysis, and as few as 3 for cardiomyocyte RNA.
Analyses at this scale are capable of detecting coordinated, pathwaylevel changes but not individual gene effects, and no gene reached an adjusted significance threshold in any contrast.
The ferroptosis and p53 effector transcripts central to our proposed mechanism, including GPX4 and TIGAR, were not detected at levels permitting testing in in cardiomyocytes.
As the analyses were only powered to detect large treatment effects (>2FC) we conclude that the transcriptomic data can neither support nor exclude regulation of these pathways in myocardium.

text.text: A final limitation is that right atrial biopsies have indirect generalisability to ventricular tissue.

However, in our experience, the routine collection of adequate quantities of atrial myocardium is more consistent and reproducible than for ventricular tissue which is a key consideration in experimental RCTs where the numbers of participants are limited.
Pre-surgery administration of sodium valproate 15mg/kg/day ≤14 days is safe and well tolerated in cardiac surgery patients.
The direction of the treatment effect on myocardial injury in vivo was consistent with myocardial protection.

Multilevel characterisation of myocardial biopsies collected at surgery suggest post-translational effectors, including pAKT-GSK3β activation, and p53 acetylation/GPX4 prevention of post IRI ferroptosis as likely mechanisms.
Longer duration treatment likely increased myocardial injury susceptibility via cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation and activation of pro-apoptotic, ferroptotic, and necroptotic signaling networks.
